transcript: Sometimes a play really toes the line between being urgently relevant and too close for comfort. The Antiquities by Jordan Harrison is such an example. This piece, currently being presented at Playwrights Horizons, is a slow burn of a science fiction drama, with the concept being an exhibition of humanity through a timeline from the 1800s into the far future where humans no longer exist. The years and scenes feature various technological advancements as we were developing them. I think the play pretty explicitly alludes to how our human desire to innovate is natural and inevitable, but also reckless and at our own peril. What I appreciate about this play in retrospect is how smartly it’s structured — not just the content of the scenes, but also the sequencing of the scenes which is a huge part of what makes the play land. But I have to say, this was not a comfortable watch. It was definitely unsettling with its overall pessimistic, stark, and sterile aesthetic and thesis. It’s one of those pieces that I'm glad I saw, but I only need to experience once — take with that what you will.
reasoning: The reviewer appreciates the structure and relevance but describes it as uncomfortable, unsettling, and a 'one and done' experience, landing between recommendation and reservation.
